description: Wanna be farmer interested in the improvement of human life on our planet.
summary:
FieldShift is a free web app that turns NASA and ESA data into plain, explained crop decisions for one farmer’s own field. The farmer draws the field on a satellite map, says what he grew and what matters to him (water, soil, income, fewer bad years), and gets a clear answer in about a minute: what to sow next, when to sow it, and what it earns in a normal and a bad year.

Behind the answer, FieldShift stress-tests 24 crops against 24 years of NASA POWER weather on that exact field: rain at sowing, water through winter and spring, and heat in the sensitive months. It projects how this changes by 2035, and reads 5 years of Sentinel-2 imagery inside the field outline to show bare soil, moisture and crop growth. We back-tested the model against the Bulgarian Ministry of Agriculture’s report on the 2020 Dobrudzha drought, when wheat yields fell 68%.

This addresses the Field Shift challenge directly: farmers adapting to a drier, hotter climate get rotation strategies built on the data, explained in their own terms, instead of raw satellite layers they can’t use.
details:
What it does
FieldShift helps a farmer decide what to grow next on a specific field as the climate shifts. It works in four steps:

  1. Pick the field: search a village and draw the field on a satellite map of Bulgaria.
  2. Tell us about you: enter the last 5 seasons’ crops (or choose “starting out”) and pick priorities from 12 options: moisture, erosion, income, soil health, fewer bad years, costs, labour, machinery, market, animal feed, pests, EU subsidies.
  3. Live analysis: the server fetches every data source for that exact field shape and shows each step as it happens.
    • one clear answer: what to sow next and when, with three reasons and the main risk;
    • three rotation strategies compared in euros per decare for a normal and a bad year;
    • plain-language insight cards (bare soil days, moisture vs earlier years, dry summers, warming, slope);
    • satellite checks of what really grew each year;
    • pests to watch and fertilizer needs;
    • weather alerts in four levels (urgent alerts by automated call and SMS).

How it works

  • Stress test: each of 24 crops is checked against every past season on the field’s own weather. It must have enough rain at sowing, enough water from October through its sensitive months (at least 80% of that field’s own normal), enough season water including soil storage, and no heat stress.
  • 2035 outlook: past weather is shifted along the measured temperature and rain trends.
  • Season risk: an analog-year model compares this season so far with the 24 past ones.
  • Satellite indices: NDVI, SAVI, NDMI and a Bare Soil Index from Sentinel-2, cloud-masked and averaged inside the field outline.
  • Validation: we tested the model against the Ministry of Agriculture’s 2019/2020 agrometeorological report. NASA POWER rain matched the General Toshevo station in most months. Our first model wrongly called 2020 a good wheat year, so we found the cause (it assumed the soil was always full after a dry winter) and fixed it. The app lets anyone check any past year themselves.

Benefits and impact
Farmers can see their crops, but not 24 years of weather risk, bare-soil days or the 2035 trend. FieldShift turns free public data into a decision a farmer can act on and check. It’s honest when the current rotation already fits, instead of pushing change.

Tools

  • Node.js and Express on the server, vanilla JavaScript in the browser.
  • Leaflet and Leaflet-Geoman for the map, Chart.js for the charts.
  • Hosted on Render.
  • Caching, data validation and 47 automated tests.
  • Graceful fallbacks when a data service is slow or down.

Creativity and factors we considered

  • Bulgarian units (decares) and euros, with Bulgarian crop names accepted.
  • SMS alerts, because they work on weak 2G signal in rural areas.
  • The farmer’s own yields and prices can replace our regional estimates.
  • A clear statement that FieldShift supports, not replaces, the local agronomist.
